text.p: A federal judge Thursday sentenced former Lazard Freres & Co. partner Mark Ferber to 33 months in prison and a $1 million fine for fraud and corruption before delivering a scathing assessment of the municipal bond industry.
U.S. District Judge William Young at one point likened Lazard Freres's attitude to the refrain sung by a robber in the Broadway hit "Les Miserables": "What do I care? Give me my share."
In a separate action, the Securities and Exchange Commission said Ferber agreed to pay $650,000 in fines and be permanently barred from the $1.3 trillion municipal bond market.

The 43-year-old lawyer and financial adviser was convicted in August on 58 of 61 counts of fraud and corruption involving a contract he maintained with Merrill Lynch & Co. to advise government clients in the municipal bond market.

The charges centred on whether the contract was adequately disclosed to Ferber's government clients, for whom he was supposed to be acting as an independent financial adviser. Those clients included the District of Columbia and the Massachusetts Water Resources Authority.
Merrill Lynch and Lazard settled with the U.S. attorney's office last last year, paying $24 million in fines with neither firm admitting or denying guilt.

But Young, who called Ferber "an obviously brilliant man ... with a tragic flaw," appeared annoyed that Merrill Lynch "bought its way out for $12 million. ... I don't think the $12 million settlement caused them much pain on their way to the tennis courts ..."

Merrill Lynch spokesman Timothy Gilles said, "We strongly disagree with the judge's characterisations, which are unfortunate and unfair. Merrill Lynch's record for integrity and upholding the highest standards of business conduct has been well established over decades."

Young also lashed into Ferber's former employer, saying, "Lazard Freres was totally bereft of internal quality controls. Their attitude can be summed up ... by the robber in 'Les Miserables' who sings, 'What do I care? Give me my share.'"
"At least they (Lazard Freres) had the decency ... to get out of the municipal bond business," Young said.

Lazard in a statement said, "Lazard has a documented 150-year history of integrity and quality in representing our clients. The unauthoritzed activites of a former member of our firm, for which we have paid a heavy price, are highly regrettable: they will in no way change our continued commitment to the qualities that have enabled us to maintain our distinguished position over this long period of time."
Ferber, his stocky frame crammed into a blue suit, sat impassively in court as the judge railed against the industry, including municipal bond lawyers.

In addition to the 33-month prison sentence, $1 million fine and $1,150 in court costs, Ferber will have to serve two years probation. He is expected to report to a low-security federal prison in northern central Pennsylvania Jan. 14.
With time off for good behaviour, Ferber could be eligible for parole in about 30 months.

Assistant U.S. Attorney Brien O'Connor said the Ferber prosecution "has already had an effect on the industry." His co-counsel, David Apfel, said, "We know this case has been discussed in California and Chicago. It has had an impact."
The head of the Securities and Exchange Commission's Boston district office, Juan Marcelino, called the settlement agreement with Ferber another warning to the municipal bond market.
"This matter demonstrates the commission's concern regarding abusive practices in the municipal industry," Marcelino said.
